method: Head-to-head. Path A: non-English prompt straight to the model, answer in the same language. Path B: prompt translated to English, model answers in English, answer translated back. Every token on both paths is counted, including the translator's own calls.
headline: Across six prompts the proxy cost 6.9% MORE than not using it. Only Korean bounded questions won clearly. The break-even model (English reply must be >=38% shorter on this model pair) predicted 5 of 6 outcomes correctly.
caveat: Four of six replies hit max_tokens. A truncated reply is pinned to the same length in both languages, so it cannot shrink and the fee buys nothing. Real savings depend on answers finishing naturally.

followup_bounded_untruncated.note: Second run correcting two flaws in the first: prompts that ask for a bounded answer, and a ceiling high enough that nothing truncates. Four of six saved money, versus one of six before. The earlier -6.9% total was driven by truncation and open-ended prompts, not by language. Japanese in particular went from losing to saving 31% once its answer was allowed to finish.

summarization_control.question: Is the saving real tokenization efficiency, or is the English answer simply a thinner answer? (i.e. summarization wearing a translation costume)
summarization_control.method: Same question asked in Korean and in English with an identical explicit format instruction (markdown numbered list, exactly three items, one sentence each), so neither model can win by answering less.
summarization_control.finding: English delivered 43% MORE text using 65% FEWER tokens. A summarization effect would have produced less text, not more. The 4.1x gap is the tokenizer, not the content.
summarization_control.caveat: Uncontrolled, some of the saving IS content loss: in a free-form comparison the round-tripped Korean answer lost a concrete example and all markdown structure (heading, numbered list), delivering 37% fewer characters. Five of five substantive facts survived. So translation genuinely compresses, but the round trip can also flatten formatting and drop illustrative detail.

formatting_preservation.question: Can the lost structure be restored, and what does it cost?
formatting_preservation.method: The translator was already preserving markdown faithfully; the loss came from the model formatting differently when answering in English. Fixed by instructing the model, not the translator. Same question, three paths.
formatting_preservation.finding: The instruction restores the heading and delivers 458 chars, MORE than the native answer's 354, while still using 36% fewer output tokens. Bullets replaced the numbered list, so the shape is close but not identical.
formatting_preservation.cost: Savings drop from 67% to 36% of native output tokens. That is the price of not silently flattening the answer, and it is on by default because quietly degrading output is not a trade users opted into.

instruction_tuning.question: Can the instruction be sharpened to also restore numbered lists?
instruction_tuning.finding: Naming the mirroring rule ('if it asks for N points, use a numbered list') matched the native shape on 2 of 3 prompts against 1 of 3 for the first version, and used fewer tokens doing it.
instruction_tuning.limit: Exact shape matching is not achievable and is the wrong target: the native answer is itself inconsistent, using a heading for the Korean list question and none for the same question in Japanese. The goal is a structured answer, not a byte-identical one.
